source_read: PDF, pp. 542-550 (all pages; Tables 1-4 and Figures 1-2 checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi, Figure 2 at 300 dpi)

claims.overstatement: All figures are shares of offices, not of deaths, and come from self-report. 'Coroners or other non-physicians most often decided which deaths were tested (64.7%)' means 64.7% of offices that request toxicology named a coroner/non-physician among those who decide (check all that apply), more than any other role; it is not the share of deaths. '11.2% had none' is as reported: the authors note such offices may have their cases tested through an autopsy provider or state office, and flag possible misclassification of the no-access and not-needed answers. The sentence implies all percentages are of the 1,320; the screening figures are of 1,326 and 709.
claims.note: Checked and recomputed: 1,320; 82.6% = (78 + 1,012)/1,320 = 82.58% (sum of printed 5.9% and 76.7%); 11.2%, 6.2%; 96.4% and 75.1% (no counts printed, cannot recompute); 64.7% (Figure 2, 300 dpi); 53.9% = 715/1,326; 95.1% = 674/709. The statement that the number of suspected overdose deaths tested is unknown is on p. 548.

anchors.locator: Materials and methods › 2018 CMEC data collection, 1st paragraph (continued) and Measures, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: 2018 Census of Medical Examiner and Coroner Offices (collected June 2019-March 2020): 1,648 of 2,037 offices responded (80.9%); long form 1,341 (81.4%), short form 307 (18.6%); BJS hot-deck imputations for non-response are in the public file and were used. Offices grouped by question C12 (N = 1,320): whether the office primarily provides toxicology internally, externally, has no access, or does not need it.

anchors.locator: Results › MEC characteristics by toxicology capabilities, 1st paragraph; Table 1
anchors.extracted: Of 1,320 offices: internal toxicology 78 (5.9%), external 1,012 (76.7%), no access 148 (11.2%), not needed 82 (6.2%); access 1,090/1,320 = 82.6% (recomputed; Discussion says about 83%); no access or not needed 230 (17.4%). Access by population served: small (24,999 or fewer; n = 550) 75.1%, large (250,000 or more; n = 195) 96.4% (medium n = 575, value not given); chi = 29.88, P < 0.001. Shares of offices, not of deaths.

anchors.locator: Results › Determination of toxicology testing need, 1st paragraph; Figure 2
anchors.extracted: Check-all-that-apply question on who decides which cases get toxicology (n = 1,340; only offices that request toxicology shown): coroner/non-physician 64.7%, autopsy pathologist 27.0%, death investigator 24.4%; offices with internal toxicology 41.0%, 60.3%, 16.7%; with external toxicology 67.5%, 27.5%, 25.5% (Figure 2 read at 300 dpi). Shares of offices naming each role, not shares of deaths.

anchors.locator: Results › Forensic toxicology testing strategy, 1st paragraph; Table 3 (p. 546)
anchors.extracted: Drug screening tests at the scene, external examination or autopsy: 53.9% (715 of 1,326 responding offices); of these 95.1% (674 of 709 valid responses) routinely confirm with laboratory toxicology (both recomputed). Denominators are 1,326 and 709, not 1,320. Testing strategy changed because of the opioid epidemic in 57.4% (761/1,326).

About 83% of offices report access, over 1 in 10 none. Authors: offices reporting no access may have their cases processed through an autopsy provider or state medical examiner office; some serve rural or frontier areas with few deaths (about 300 offices reported five or fewer deaths a year; 46% of all offices served under 25,000 people, per the BJS report).

anchors.locator: Discussion › 6th paragraph (sentence at top of p. 548)
anchors.extracted: Authors state that the annual number of suspected overdose cases that receive toxicology testing is unknown, even in offices with in-house testing, and that data from at least two states indicate testing is not done at the level needed.

Voluntary survey; the toxicology-capability question was open to interpretation (some offices may have counted drug screens as toxicology); 43 of the 230 offices reporting no access or no need said testing decisions were not made by their office, while 187 (about 14% of offices) named staff who decide, suggesting misclassification; paper-form skip patterns not always followed.

claims.overstatement: The 'about 80% in coroner systems' figure is quoted by the paper from the BJS report on the same census, not computed by these authors. The size comparison (75.1% against 96.4%) is by population served; the paper does not compare toxicology access between coroner and medical-examiner systems, so it is context, not evidence that coroner systems test less. 64.7% is a share of offices (check all that apply), not of deaths.
claims.note: Numbers 80%, 64.7%, 75.1%, 96.4% checked on the rendered pages (pp. 544-545).

anchors.locator: Results › Determination of toxicology testing need, 1st paragraph; Figure 2 (p. 545)
anchors.extracted: Coroners (Figure 2 label: coroner/non-physician) were most often named as deciding which cases get toxicology (64.7% of offices, check all that apply); the authors say this agrees with the BJS census report that 80% of offices were within a coroner system (cited from ref. 2, not computed in this paper). Autopsy pathologists were named more often where toxicology is internal (60.3%), coroners where it is external (67.5%).

anchors.locator: Results › MEC characteristics by toxicology capabilities, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Access to toxicology 75.1% in offices serving 24,999 or fewer (n = 550) against 96.4% in offices serving 250,000 or more (n = 195); chi = 29.88, P < 0.001. The paper compares access by population served, not by medical-examiner versus coroner system.

Voluntary survey; the toxicology-capability question was open to interpretation (some offices may have counted drug screens as toxicology); 43 of the 230 offices reporting no access or no need said testing decisions were not made by their office, while 187 (about 14% of offices) named staff who decide, suggesting misclassification; paper-form skip patterns not always followed.

key_findings.correction: 23/78 = 29.5% and 16/78 = 20.5% recomputed; the printed 29.4% is a rounding error.
Figure 2 re-read at 300 dpi. Weighted internal and external averages recomputed: about 29.8%, 65.6% and 24.9%.
Incompatibility recomputed: (0.208 x 1,012 + at most 0.02 x 308)/1,320 is at most 16.4%.

reporting_issues.note: Confirmed as printed. The two figures use different cut-offs (zero to four deaths against five or fewer) and possibly different bases (1,341 long-form offices against all offices), so the mismatch may be one of definition rather than an error.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor: the abstract matches the tables, and the errors are in the Discussion's context figures.

missed: pp. 546-547, Discussion 1st paragraph: the authors say offices reporting no access to toxicology may have their cases processed through an autopsy provider or a state medical examiner office, and some serve rural or frontier areas with few deaths. 'No access' (11.2%) therefore does not mean that the deaths were not tested. This matters for claims citing the 11.2%.
p. 543, Measures: question C12i asks how the office primarily provides toxicology, so each category records the office's main route only.
